html:
A caliphate of Ismaili Shia Muslims that ruled North Africa, Egypt and at times Syria and the Hejaz from 909 to 1171. Its rulers claimed descent from Fatima, the Prophet's daughter, and set themselves up as rival caliphs to the Abbasids of Baghdad.

The movement started as a secret missionary network. In 909 it took power in Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia), backed by Kutama Berber tribesmen. In 969 its army under the general Jawhar took Egypt, and next to the old capital he laid out a new palace city, Cairo. The mosque of al-Azhar followed in 970 and grew into one of the oldest working universities.

Egypt under the Fatimids was rich. Red Sea trade with India ran through it, and Cairo became the great city of the Islamic Mediterranean. The rulers were Shia, but most of their subjects stayed Sunni, and Christians and Jews often served in government.

Some moments:

  • The caliph al-Hakim (996 to 1021) was erratic and harsh; the Druze faith grew from followers who saw him as divine.
  • When their governors in Tunisia broke away, the Fatimids are said to have sent the Arab Banu Hilal tribes west to punish them.
  • They lost Jerusalem to the First Crusade in 1099.

The state then weakened under feuding viziers. In 1171 Saladin, vizier for the last caliph, ended the dynasty and brought Egypt back to Sunni Islam under the Ayyubids.
